title: Neither coming nor going (section 29)
hook: the Tathagata neither comes nor goes; that is why he is called the Tathagata

segments.voice: Yesterday, merit not held: the bodhisattva gains merit and doesn't take hold of it. Your line: not held. Which good deed did you let run on like water? Day one thousand one hundred forty-six.

A map app runs on two questions. Where are you? Where are you going? A blue dot, a line, a time to arrival, and at the end a cheerful voice: you have arrived. Then, a few minutes later, a new destination. Whole days can be lived inside that blue dot, always on the way, rarely there. The Diamond Sutra opened with the Buddha on the move: walking into town for alms, walking back, sitting down. Now, near the end, section twenty-nine says something that seems to erase the whole walk. Today: neither coming nor going.
screen: `WHERE ARE YOU? WHERE TO?` → `YOU HAVE ARRIVED. AGAIN.` → `THE WALK, ERASED?`

segments.voice: First, the claim. The Buddha tells Subhuti, in paraphrase: if anyone says the Tathagata comes or goes, or stands, or sits, or lies down, that person hasn't understood what I teach. Coming, going, standing, sitting, lying down: the sutra lists the ordinary shapes of a body's day, and then says the Tathagata isn't to be pinned to any of them. Second, the puzzle. We watched him do every one of those things. Back in section one he walked to town with his bowl, ate, came back, washed his feet and sat down. The sutra isn't taking that back. The body walked. The question is whether the one called Tathagata is that walking. Third, the reason the sutra gives. The Tathagata, it says, doesn't go anywhere and doesn't come from anywhere, and that is exactly why he is called the Tathagata. The sutra hands the title its own meaning. Not a traveler who arrived somewhere special. Not a visitor who will one day leave. What the name points to was never on the road. It's the same cut as the verse about form and sound, made one step deeper: not the body's shape, and not the body's movements either. Fourth, why it lands on an ordinary day. So much of a life is spent in transit, in the head if not on the road. Almost there. Not yet. Next. Section twenty-nine doesn't tell anyone to stop walking. The dishes still need doing and the bus still leaves at eight. It points at something in the middle of all the walking that isn't going anywhere, and asks you to notice it once.
screen: `COMES, GOES, STANDS, SITS, LIES DOWN.` · `BUT WE WATCHED HIM WALK.` · `GOES NOWHERE, COMES FROM NOWHERE.` · `STILL IN THE MIDDLE OF THE WALK.` · then, large: `NEITHER COMING NOR GOING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like: rest in not going anywhere. Settle, and breathe. Notice where your mind is headed: the next task, tonight, tomorrow. Don't push it away. Just see the blue dot moving. Then let the destination go for a moment. There's nowhere this breath has to take you. The breath comes, the breath goes, and the knowing of it stays right here. Rest in that. If the mind leaves for somewhere, notice it went, and come back without scolding. Nothing to arrive at for these two minutes. The bell holds the time.
Neither coming nor going. Section twenty-nine: the Tathagata goes nowhere and comes from nowhere, and that is why he is called the Tathagata. Today's word.
Your line: neither coming nor going. Today, on one walk or drive, let yourself be fully where you are for a moment, instead of almost there. Day one thousand one hundred forty-six.

howItsDone: Mahayana Buddhists who study the Diamond Sutra read section 29 as the sutra's own gloss on the title Tathagata.

fork.setup: someone says: the Tathagata came to town, then went back to the grove. what does section 29 say about that person?
options: they should add that he sat down
fork.reveal: anyone who says the Tathagata comes, goes, stands, sits or lies down hasn't understood: he goes nowhere and comes from nowhere.

original.note: Sanskrit and Pali: the title the Buddha uses for himself; section 29 explains it as one who neither comes nor goes.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Buddha never really walked anywhere.
what it means: the body walked; what the name Tathagata points to was never on the road.
what a scholar hears: section 29 lists coming, going, standing, sitting and lying down, then makes the title itself mean 'goes nowhere, comes from nowhere.'
